title: After a Nationwide Flight Standstill, a $50 Billion Question
summary: Last Friday, air travel across the United States came to a standstill for more than four hours. It was the longest nationwide ground stop since the attacks of September 11, 2001, and it turned the whole weekend into a travel headache, with cancellations and long delays at airports everywhere. By Monday, planes were back in the skies and travel was slowly returning to normal. But the big question had only just begun: how do you fix a system this old, and who pays for it? Investigators are still digging into what went wrong. The Trump administration says the trouble started at a single air traffic control facility in southern Arkansas, where a government contractor was replacing aging copper wire communication lines with fiber. A network router there was flooded with thousands of data pings every few seconds, overloading the systems controllers use to guide pilots. The problem may then have spread to a router in Texas. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the equipment as very, very old, saying it had suffered a kind of heart attack. He said the system is on average about 50 years old, and procedures for doing this kind of work will be reviewed so it cannot bring the system down again. He also stressed that nobody was hurt and no planes crashed. Now a funding fight is brewing. Secretary Duffy is asking Congress for $50 billion to upgrade the nation's air traffic control systems. Democrats are pushing back, saying billions of dollars have already been approved for an overhaul of the Federal Aviation Administration, and they want answers about where that money went. Travelers, meanwhile, just want to get home after a weekend of cancellations.
why_it_matters: Air travel is how many families visit relatives and go on trips, so a broken control system can strand travelers across the whole country.

background_read: Air traffic control is the system that keeps planes safe in the sky.
Controllers on the ground talk to pilots and tell each plane where to go, so planes do not get too close to each other.
The system uses radios, computers and radar, and much of its equipment is very old.
When one part of the system fails, flights across the whole country can be delayed or stopped.
